{{Short description|Governance of the Northwest Territories}}
The '''politics of the Northwest Territories''' involves not only the governance of the [[Northwest Territories]] but also the social, economic and political issues specific to the [[Provinces and territories of Canada|territory]]. This includes matters relating to local governance and governance by the [[Government of Canada|federal government]] of [[Canada]], the inclusion of the [[Aboriginal peoples in Canada|aboriginal]] population in territorial affairs, and the matter of official languages for the territory.

Key to the politics and governance of the Northwest Territories are the limits on the jurisdiction of the territorial government. Territories of Canada have no [[inherent jurisdiction]] and only have those powers [[Devolution|devolved]] to them by the federal government.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Northwest Territories Act|year=1985 |url=http://laws.justice.gc.ca/en/N-27/252179.html |author=Department of Justice Canada|access-date=January 27, 2007}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://laws.justice.gc.ca/en/Y-2.01/265655.html|title=Yukon Act|year=2002|author=Department of Justice Canada|access-date=January 27, 2007}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://laws.justice.gc.ca/en/N-28.6/index.html|title=Nunavut Act|year=1993|author=Department of Justice Canada|access-date=January 27, 2007}}</ref> The devolution and delegation of power to the territory has always been a factor in the territory's politics.

A hallmark of politics in the Northwest Territories is that it operates as under a “[[Consensus government in Canada|consensus government]]” system.<ref name=":0">{{Cite news |last=Williams |first=Ollie |date=2025-02-12 |title=Testart, other MLAs to propose 'elements of party politics' |url=https://cabinradio.ca/222741/news/politics/testart-other-mlas-to-propose-elements-of-party-politics/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250214153331/https://cabinradio.ca/222741/news/politics/testart-other-mlas-to-propose-elements-of-party-politics/ |archive-date=2025-02-14 |access-date=2025-03-20 |work=[[Cabin Radio]]}}</ref> Candidates for election to the territorial legislature do not stand as members of a [[List of political parties in Canada|political party]].<ref name=":0" /> While some candidates may express an affiliation or membership with a party, party membership is not recognized in the legislature.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Danylchuk |first=Jack |date=2015-01-27 |title=Consensus government not working in the N.W.T. |url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/north/consensus-government-not-working-in-the-n-w-t-1.2933426 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150128205033/https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/north/consensus-government-not-working-in-the-n-w-t-1.2933426 |archive-date=2015-01-28 |access-date=2025-03-20 |work=CBC News}}</ref> As a result, the [[Member of the Legislative Assembly|Members of the Legislative Assembly]] select a [[Premier of the Northwest Territories|Premier]] by way of a [[secret ballot]], rather than on the basis of party affiliation (see [[Responsible government]]).<ref>{{Cite news |last=Williams |first=Ollie |date=2023-11-30 |title=How can the NWT get a better government off the ground? |url=https://cabinradio.ca/163185/news/politics/how-can-the-nwt-get-a-better-government-off-the-ground/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240123115217/https://cabinradio.ca/163185/news/politics/how-can-the-nwt-get-a-better-government-off-the-ground/ |archive-date=2024-01-23 |access-date=2023-11-30 |work=[[Cabin Radio]]}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Carroll |first=Luke |date=2023-10-20 |title=Should the public know who their MLA voted for as N.W.T. premier? |url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/north/nwt-mla-vote-premier-public-1.7002772 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231208034116/https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/north/nwt-mla-vote-premier-public-1.7002772 |archive-date=2023-12-08 |access-date=2025-03-20 |work=CBC News}}</ref>

Local governance has been a long-standing issue in the territory. This includes not only the loss of local government authority from the period from 1905 to 1951, when Ottawa asserted direct control over the governance of the territory, but also related matters of aboriginal [[Indigenous self-government in Canada|self-governance]] and [[Indigenous land claims in Canada|land claims]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Bartlett |first=Richard |date=1978-10-01 |title=The Indian Act of Canada |url=https://digitalcommons.law.buffalo.edu/buffalolawreview/vol27/iss4/3/ |journal=Buffalo Law Review |volume=27 |issue=4 |pages=581 |issn=0023-9356}}</ref> This latter issue lead, in part, to the division of the territory into the Northwest Territories and [[Nunavut]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Dacks |first=Gurston |date=1986 |title=The Case against Dividing the Northwest Territories |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/3550729 |journal=Canadian Public Policy / Analyse de Politiques |volume=12 |issue=1 |pages=202–213 |doi=10.2307/3550729 |jstor=3550729 |issn=0317-0861|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Abele |first1=Frances |last2=Dickerson |first2=Mark O. |date=1985 |title=The 1982 Plebiscite on Division of the Northwest Territories: Regional Government and Federal Policy |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/3550376 |journal=Canadian Public Policy / Analyse de Politiques |volume=11 |issue=1 |pages=1–15 |doi=10.2307/3550376 |jstor=3550376 |issn=0317-0861|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Légaré |first=André |date=2008-09-01 |title=Inuit identity and regionalization in the Canadian Central and Eastern Arctic: a survey of writings about Nunavut |url=https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/10889370701742845 |journal=Polar Geography |volume=31 |issue=3–4 |pages=99–118 |doi=10.1080/10889370701742845 |issn=1088-937X}}</ref>

Language has also been a long-standing issue in Northwest Territory politics. [[French language|French]] became an official language, along with [[English language|English]], in 1877.<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |last=Aunger |first=Edmund A. |date=1998 |title=The Mystery of the French Language Ordinances: An Investigation into Official Bilingualism and the Canadian North-West—1870 to 1895 |url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/product/identifier/S0829320100005597/type/journal_article |journal=Canadian Journal of Law and Society |language=en |volume=13 |issue=1 |pages=89–124 |doi=10.1017/S0829320100005597 |issn=0829-3201|url-access=subscription }}</ref> This resulted in heated debates in the territorial assembly and the establishment of English as the only official language until pressure from the federal government in the 1980s lead to not only the inclusion of French as an official language, but also nine aboriginal languages.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Tessier-Burns |first=Francis |date=2024-05-02 |title=The N.W.T. has 11 official languages, yet service in Indigenous languages continues to be a struggle |url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/north/more-services-needed-in-official-languages-nwt-1.7129999 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240410173733/https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/north/more-services-needed-in-official-languages-nwt-1.7129999 |archive-date=2024-04-10 |access-date=2025-03-20 |work=CBC News}}</ref><ref name=":1" />
